answer: Every agent's vote is split across two disjoint shards drawn from its settlement history. One shard attests a decision; a second, whose members the identity cannot pick, audits five percent of it, and any contradiction burns both deposits. A sybil cluster must plant capital in every shard it wants to sway, where independent members outnumber it, so an alias costs a real counterparty network instead of a key pair. Newcomers start thin, like yarrow on stony ground, earning seats through settled trades; clones stay as uniform as sable and as brittle as juniper, collapsing at the first audit.
